To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) C3 grasses have lower photosynthetic rates than C4 grasses in mesocosms, 2) C3 grass photosynthetic rates decline with soil water availability, 3) C4 grasses have higher photosynthetic water-use efficiency than C3 grasses in mesocoms, and 4) C3 and C3 grasses do not differ significantly in photosynthetic rates or water-use efficiency in the field.
C4 grasses have higher intrinsic photosynthetic rates in mesocosms but that these advantages disappear when plants are grown in the field.

C4 grasses have higher intrinsic photosynthetic rates than C3 species in resource-rich environments, but this difference is absent in resource-poor field settings where photosynthetic rate is not limited by resources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physiological mechanisms that contribute to species diversity and productivity in grassland ecosystems.
the role of photosynthesis in the ecology of C4 plants in grassland ecosystems.
the physiological basis for dominance of C4 grasses in the North American tallgrass (NTG) prairie, an ecosystem composed of a diverse mixture of C3 and 4 grasses and forbs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
C4 plants have an advantage in the tallgrass prairie, but that this advantage is not always expressed in photosynthetic rate and is not always expressed at the leaf level.
(1) In mesocosms, photosynthetic rates of C4 grasses are higher than those of C3 grasses, (2) In the field, photosynthetic rate of C4 grass is not higher than that of C3 grass.
C4 grasses are more tolerant to resource limitations, but that the C4 advantage may not be as strong in the field as in the mesocosms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the C3 species were not able to compete with the C4 species in terms of photosynthetic rates and water use efficiency in a mesocosm environment.
the intrinsic photosynthetic differences between C3 species and C4 grass species are consistent with the dominance of C3 species in the mesocosms.
the photosynthetic advantages of C4 grasses are not sufficient to explain their dominance of North American tallgrass ecosystems.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the C4 grasses in the mesocosm were able to grow rapidly when conditions were optimal (i.e. when resources were plentiful), but they were not able to maintain that rapid growth when the environment became more limiting.
C4 species are not necessarily better at using water or light than C3 species.
photosynthetic traits measured in mesocosms may not be predictive of species dominance in natural ecosystems.
